title: Forwarded Records in Heaps
description: Forwarded records in a heap make a scan chase pointers across pages; rebuilding the heap removes the forwarding. Why it matters: forwarded records are a slow, silent tax that accumulates on heaps under update-heavy workloads -- exactly the kind of issue that goes unnoticed until someone finally investigates "why do simple scans read so much."
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
Every SQL Server table's rows live on fixed-size 8KB pages, like sheets of paper in a filing cabinet where each sheet only has room for so many entries. A table can be organized in one of two basic ways. A **clustered index** keeps rows physically sorted by a key, like a phone book sorted by last name — very orderly, and moving a row generally means keeping that order intact. A **heap** is the other option: a table with no clustered index, where SQL Server just puts each row wherever there happens to be free space, with no particular ordering at all, more like a box where you toss papers in wherever there's room. Heaps are simpler and can be faster for pure insert-heavy workloads, but they come with a specific, easy-to-overlook cost that this lesson is about: what happens when a row in a heap needs to grow.

Suppose a row starts out small — maybe it has a `Notes` column that's currently empty or short — and it gets placed on a page alongside a bunch of other small rows, filling that page up nicely. Later, someone runs an UPDATE that fills in a much longer `Notes` value for that row. The row is now bigger than it used to be, and there may not be enough leftover space on its original page to let it grow in place — its neighbors are still sitting right next to it with no gap to expand into. In a clustered index, SQL Server can perform a **page split**: it takes the overflowing page and divides its contents across two pages, making room. But a heap has no ordering to preserve, so instead of splitting, SQL Server does something more localized: it **moves the entire row to a different page** that has enough free space, and it leaves behind, in the row's *original* location, a small stub called a **forwarding pointer** — literally just a note that says 'this row actually now lives over on page X.' The row's physical address changes, but nothing that points *to* the row (like a nonclustered index entry) gets updated to know that — updating every reference everywhere would be expensive, so SQL Server instead leaves a forwarding pointer as a cheap redirect.

Here's where the performance problem creeps in. When SQL Server needs to scan the *whole* heap — for something as innocent-looking as `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders` — it walks through the table's pages in physical allocation order, one after another. When it lands on a slot that has been forwarded, it can't just skip it; it has to actually **follow the pointer**, jump to wherever the row now lives, read it from there, and then come back and continue the scan where it left off. Every single forwarded row costs an *extra* page read beyond what a normal scan would need. Picture flipping through a filing cabinet where, every so often, instead of a real page, you find a sticky note saying 'see page 400 instead' — you now have to go find page 400, read it, and come back, over and over, on top of your normal flip-through. If a meaningful fraction of the rows in a table have been forwarded — say, 50,000 out of a few hundred thousand — the number of extra 'go read this other page instead' detours starts to add up to a genuinely large multiple of the reads a clean scan would need, even though the table's actual data size hasn't changed at all.

Why does this happen so often in real systems, and why does it sneak up on people? Because the pattern that causes it — insert rows small, then later fill in a big optional column via a batch job or a later workflow step — is an extremely common, completely reasonable application design. Think of an order that starts with just the basics, and later has customer support notes, a long shipping-exception explanation, or an attached comment added to it after the fact. Nobody designs a table intending to create forwarded records; they accumulate silently, one UPDATE at a time, as a natural side effect of how the application actually uses the table over its lifetime. And because a forwarded record doesn't cause any error or wrong result — the query still returns the correct count, the correct rows, everything is logically fine — this kind of bloat is invisible unless someone actually goes looking for it. It just shows up as 'huh, this really simple COUNT(*) is oddly slow for how few rows this table has,' which is exactly the kind of mystery that often goes uninvestigated for a long time.

The way to actually detect this is to check a system function called `sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats`, which reports a `forwarded_record_count` for heaps — a direct, named count of exactly how many forwarding pointers exist right now. You can also spot the symptom indirectly by comparing the logical reads reported by `STATISTICS IO` against the table's real page count: if reads are running several times higher than the actual number of pages the table occupies, forwarded records chasing is a prime suspect. And critically, this problem is *specific to heaps* — it cannot happen in a clustered index at all, because a clustered index handles growing rows via page splits instead of forwarding. That gives two possible fixes: either periodically **rebuild the heap** (`ALTER TABLE ... REBUILD`), which physically relocates every row into fresh, compact pages and resets the forwarded-record count back to zero, or add a **clustered index** to the table so it becomes an ordered b-tree structure that doesn't produce forwarding pointers in the first place.

## Scenario
`Orders` is a **heap** (no clustered index). It was loaded with tiny rows, then a batch job filled in a large `Notes` column on about half of them. Now a simple `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Orders` reads *far* more pages than the table actually occupies.

## Why it's slow
When you enlarge a variable-length column in a heap and the row no longer fits on its page, SQL Server moves the row to a new page and leaves a **forwarding pointer** in the original slot. A scan that hits the old slot must **follow the pointer** to the forwarded row (an extra read) and then continue. With ~50,000 forwarded records, the allocation-order scan does roughly **4× the logical reads** of the underlying pages.

## What to look for
- `sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats(...)` shows a high **`forwarded_record_count`**.
- In `STATISTICS IO`: logical reads far exceeding the table's real `page_count`.

## The concept
Forwarding only happens in **heaps**. Remove the pointers by **rebuilding the heap** (`ALTER TABLE ... REBUILD`, which relocates every row and resets `forwarded_record_count` to 0), or by adding a **clustered index** so the table becomes a b-tree that has no forwarding at all.
hints: Compare STATISTICS IO logical reads to the real page_count from sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats — the gap is the forwarding overhead.
Forwarded records exist only in heaps, created when an in-place update grows a row off its page.
Rebuild the heap to clear the forwarding pointers: ALTER TABLE Orders REBUILD;
